title: 📰 AI news · November 10
takeaway: Several stories today share one thread: access sits where nobody looks, in app code, in a role for an outside service, in a factory password. Recommendation: list where your project has hardcoded passwords and keys, and which services you gave access to your data.
cta: 🔐 Check where my keys are stored

items.title: A password to Wyndham's customer database was found in its app
items.text: A researcher found a password inside the code of Wyndham's Android app. It opened a database with names, emails, member numbers and login tokens, with millions of entries. If you have an app or a bot, anything hardcoded in it can be pulled out by anyone who has it. Check today that your code holds no passwords or keys.

items.title: Infected bee-js and Swarm Desktop stole wallet keys
items.text: Attackers used Ethersphere's own release automation to publish two malicious versions: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2. They steal the wallet key and its password and install a backdoor; the bee-js code ran by itself on install. If you install ready-made packages, a foreign version can arrive the same way. Look for these versions in your projects. Free guide "Protecting your computer, code and access": send the word "protect" to the bot.

items.title: Money stolen from Keplr wallets set up with Google or Apple login
items.text: Web3Auth, which runs the Google and Apple sign-in, had a flaw, and private keys leaked for some Keplr users. Web3Auth then emptied other at-risk wallets into recovery addresses, so an empty balance may mean the money was rescued. Wallets with a recovery phrase and hardware wallets are not affected. If your wallet uses Google or Apple login, move free funds to a wallet with a recovery phrase.

items.title: Password "admin" opened the apps of two carmakers for researchers
items.text: The login servers of two carmakers kept an admin console with the username and password admin. Through it researchers entered a customer's account, then unlocked the doors and started the engine of their own test car. Both systems were fixed about two hours after the report.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are out
items.text: Fable 5.2 is available to everyone, costs $8 per million input tokens instead of $10, and answers 30 percent faster. It scores 65 on the Artificial Analysis index, five points above Gemini 4 Carbon. Mythos 5.2 is open only to organizations that pass verification.

items.title: US regulator probes Waymo robotaxis near school buses
items.text: Almost a year ago Waymo shipped an update after cars passed stopped school buses. The regulator says most incidents happened after the update and is checking whether the fix is enough.

items.title: Fireworks AI: attackers reached customer datasets
items.text: The platform for running and fine-tuning AI models said that for some customers, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights were accessed. One route went through a third-party cloud provider. If your agents run on outside AI services, your keys live there too.

items.title: The OpenSSH flaw is being probed at scale
items.text: SANS honeypots saw the first real attempts to exploit the sshole flaw on November 5, and 713 attempts on November 6 alone. If you run your own servers with password login, check your OpenSSH version.

items.title: Meta released Muse Ember, a low-cost agent model
items.text: Ember is built for the small steps agents repeat all day. Meta says it matches Claude Haiku 5.5's best score at about a third of the cost, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens.

items.title: Nuance Labs launched Emma, a face-to-face AI
items.text: Emma talks with a face and voice at the same time. On 1,785 questions from real conversations, her reply timing matched a person's 89% of the time. You can talk to her at emma.nuancelabs.ai.
